faq_blocks.answer:
T is the first letter of Turbulent, from the NERIS Identity used by 16Personalities. It describes general self-assessment, self-assurance and sensitivity to pressure; it measures no talent, output or popularity with readers, and it is not a fifth official MBTI dimension.

After receiving feedback, record what the editor actually said, what you changed and how sure you felt about the original draft. The exercise can clarify how you respond to feedback. Your revision process cannot establish a suffix.
faq_blocks.key: What does the T in ENFP-T mean?

faq_blocks.answer:
No, they are on different layers. The third F comes from Feeling and covers judgement weighting people and values; the T on the right is Turbulent, belonging to self-assessment and pressure response.

A report that gives only four letters carries no right-hand information. Seeing -T, do not read it as Thinking either; the two Ts share a letter and belong to different frameworks.
faq_blocks.key: The third letter of ENFP-T is F. Does that conflict with the T?
faq_blocks.question: The third letter of ENFP-T is F. Does that conflict with the T?

faq_blocks.answer:
There is no such relationship. The suffix does not enter an evaluation of writing ability; whether a piece works depends on the subject, the material, the platform's standards and the editor's requirements.

The same person may rate themselves differently at the two ends while taking the same revision actions. To judge whether an edit is worth it, ask whether a reader can see a difference: the opening and conclusion deserve more work, and transitions can be let go.
faq_blocks.key: Is ENFP-T necessarily a worse writer than ENFP-A?
faq_blocks.question: Is ENFP-T necessarily a worse writer than ENFP-A?

faq_blocks.answer:
Ne or Fi strength cannot be inferred from -T. Ne and Fi are theoretical preferences in type dynamics; the NERIS Identity does not measure those two processes, and the two accounts cannot be converted into each other.

Whether the writing goes well depends on how much has been read, how much practised, and whether anyone gives specific comments, all of which can be observed separately. Spotting a function requires long-term habits of sourcing and judging; the pace of one submission is no evidence.
faq_blocks.key: Are Ne and Fi weakened in ENFP-T?

faq_blocks.answer:
Establish which layer is being sent back before touching anything.

Restate the comment, then ask one question: is the idea off, or is the opening too convoluted. The two call for different revisions, and going the wrong way wastes a whole evening. If the answer is only "it is not quite working", ask them to mark one paragraph.
faq_blocks.key: ENFP-T: when a piece is sent back, should I revise or ask first?
faq_blocks.question: ENFP-T: when a piece is sent back, should I revise or ask first?

faq_blocks.answer:
Repeated revision can help when it tests a real concern. Decide which checks the brief requires and which changes would improve the piece. A revision count tells you little about the quality of the work or the suffix.

Three columns can be listed: the argument, the examples, and the sentences that could be misread. Finish the three and submit, leaving the rest for the next piece. The next day, review by argument, evidence and risk of misreading rather than by the urge to change more.
faq_blocks.key: ENFP-T: does repeated revision count as being conscientious?
faq_blocks.question: ENFP-T: does repeated revision count as being conscientious?

faq_blocks.answer:
Yes. Getting through in one pass depends on whether the piece met the requirements; even after a rejection, a familiar subject, clear comments or enough time may leave someone little affected. Neither one-pass acceptance nor the reaction to one rejection can determine A/T.

To observe this, record the conditions at the time: how familiar the subject was, how clear the comments were, and how much time was left. With different conditions, the reaction differs anyway.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Extraversion and Introversion describe whether attention and energy tend to turn outward or inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities, while Sensing gives more weight to concrete details and experience. Feeling and Thinking describe how someone weighs people and values or impersonal criteria in decisions. Judging favors more structure in the outside world, while Perceiving favors more room to adjust.

The T on the right belongs to another layer. Identity describes general self-assessment, self-assurance and reaction to pressure; how you see your judgement after submitting a piece is only one observable scene within it, not its whole definition. It does not rate prose, topic choice or diligence.

The third letter of ENFP is F for Feeling. In other four-letter MBTI types, a T in that position stands for Thinking. The -T in ENFP-T comes from a different framework. It describes self-assurance and responses to stress.

Turbulent describes how someone may feel about their own decisions, especially under pressure. Two writers can receive the same feedback and make the same edits, yet differ in how much confidence they retain in the rest of the draft.

In the convention used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si: dominant extraverted Intuition, auxiliary introverted Feeling, tertiary Thinking written as Te, and inferior introverted Sensing. The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists Te or Ti for tertiary Thinking. The -T does not change the stack, and the stack does not prescribe the order of actions.

### How ENFP-T and ENFP-A can differ after feedback

After reviewing the same comments and making the same revision, someone closer to Turbulent may feel less sure of their original judgment. Someone closer to Assertive may still trust the parts of the draft the editor did not question. Neither response tells you whether the revision was effective.

Whether to write long or short, story or argument, depends on the material and the platform's requirements, not on the right-hand letter. The same person writing in the morning and editing someone else's draft in the afternoon has changed position, and the way they close the work does not necessarily change with it.
sections.title: ENFP-T letters and framework

sections.body_md:
In a fictional editorial review, an editor says the first three paragraphs are hard to follow. Check which paragraph they marked and whether the introduction still answers the question in the headline and brief. The same comment could point to a long setup or a mismatch with the brief. Finding out which one matters more than deciding whether to defend the draft.

The table below shows writing responses that do not separate A from T. Either end may make these choices, and the action itself is no evidence for a suffix.

| Situation | A possible choice | The cost to watch | One move to try |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Just given a topic | List the things you want to say first, then think about structure | Listing too many makes the opening wander more | After listing, circle the one most relevant to the reader's question |
| Receiving revision comments | Go through your draft point by point | The comments may mix in section preferences | Ask the editor to point at one paragraph before deciding which layer to change |
| The day before the deadline | Consider rewriting the entire draft. | A rewrite can leave too little time to check the facts. | Agree what must be fixed before submission and protect time for fact-checking. |
| The editor does not reply | Want to send another follow-up | Too many follow-ups make it hard for them to answer | Ask once, and write the question so it can be answered in one line |
| The same piece already revised several times | Want every version a little better | Returns diminish and fatigue lowers judgement | Agree with the editor in advance which items count as passing |

One counterexample is worth keeping: the same person may still feel confident about the next piece when the subject is familiar and the rejection is specific, and the same event may be read as a general rejection when the subject is unfamiliar, the comments are vague and the deadline is tight. Change the conditions and the reaction changes.
sections.title: ENFP-T core patterns, value and counterexamples

sections.body_md:
Where checking effort should go depends on whether a reader can actually see a difference after the change. Worth more revision: the opening, the conclusion, and the few sentences likely to be screenshotted and quoted. Not worth repeated work: transitions and adjectives. Separate the two and the checking has a boundary, so a whole evening does not go into adjusting the feel of one paragraph.

When an editor says you went off topic, ask them to point at one paragraph: is the example off the subject, or has the conclusion wandered onto another topic? The two corrections differ, and mixing them easily overturns the whole piece.

### ENFP-T at work or study: giving revision a finishing point

Revision exists to stop real problems, so it needs a finishing point rather than a better mood.

Before submitting, go through three columns: does the argument land on the reader's question, do the examples fit the argument (can factual cases be verified, are fictional ones marked), and is there a sentence that could be misread. Once the three are done, submit, and put the remaining ideas into a note for the next piece.

If a paper has not moved for two days, decide first whether the material is insufficient or something else interrupted; fix only one of the two, then watch for a day, and do not restructure three times in one day.

If you value detailed feedback and time to revise, compare the tasks and review cycles of roles such as content editor or research assistant. A small project or internship can show whether you want to repeat that work. The suffix cannot establish career fit.
sections.title: ENFP-T work and career exploration

sections.body_md:
Co-writing a piece, the other person says "I could not get through this section", and you may hear it first as a verdict on your prose. Restate before confirming: "did you get stuck at the third paragraph, or is the order of the whole piece wrong?" Restating pulls the scope back to a specific place.

In a fictional exchange, a friend says the draft feels long. Ask where they lost the thread. If they cannot identify a passage, you can leave the cause open or ask another reader.

If a draft receives no response, ask a specific reader one question about it. A reply gives you a point to consider. Silence does not establish what they thought of the draft.

Frequency and boundaries can be stated in advance: how often you want concentrated feedback, which changes both sides must confirm, and telling the other person early when a promised time will not be met rather than letting it run to the deadline. Agreeing costs less than guessing.

### ENFP-T: landing self-assessment back on the draft

What has to land is a location, not the strength of a feeling.

Find that specific sentence: ask the collaborator to repeat the paragraph they could not get through, and see whether they stuck on the order of information or on a premise you never stated. Once the sentence is located, the change has somewhere to go; if it cannot be located, it may only have been their state that day. Do not ask the other person to keep reassuring you that it is well written — that solves nothing and drains the relationship.
sections.title: ENFP-T relationships and communication

sections.body_md:
In a fictional publishing example, two writers look at the same numbers after releasing a piece. One may remain confident about the topic, while the other feels more doubtful about their earlier judgment. Traffic and comments can inform a review, but they cannot establish someone’s ability or which suffix fits.

The data exists to judge topics, but after a short night the same number looks more and more like a verdict. Give yourself a time limit: look for ten minutes, note what needs changing, and leave the rest for tomorrow.

Another reaction is rehearsing the readers' response for them: will they think I am preaching. The rehearsed version is usually heavier than real comments. Asking one person who will actually read it is more informative than running it repeatedly in your head.

If you have slept badly for several days, opened and closed the document again and again, and traced one rejection back to yourself repeatedly, pause the repeated rework first; if it can be negotiated, adjust the submission schedule, and talk to someone you trust. If this state persists or clearly affects daily life, consider professional support. Do not use A/T to explain insomnia.
sections.title: ENFP-T stress and recovery

sections.body_md:
Use a returned draft to reflect on three things: what the editor said, what you changed and how you felt about the original judgment afterwards. This exercise cannot establish an A/T result.

Pick a rejection you remember, and compare three things: the paragraph they named, the sentence you were most reluctant to cut, and the readers' response after the change. A change in response only shows this piece changed; whether this particular edit caused it still depends on whether other paragraphs and other readers show the same shift.

Keep counterexamples too. Some people rewrite the whole piece after one rejection yet get through in one pass on a familiar subject; others are generous with other people's drafts and severe with their own. Comparing familiarity with the subject, clarity of the feedback and the cost of rework can produce an explanation to test, not a way to type anyone.

Practise one low-risk thing: next piece, change only the opening, the conclusion and the quoted sentence, then submit. A week later, check whether the places readers got stuck were those three. If two weeks of records still show no difference, or the recording itself makes you more anxious, stop.
sections.title: ENFP-T observation practice

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The suffix follows [the 16Personalities account of NERIS](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory); the four letters and the four-position description follow the public material of the MBTI framework, and this page introduces no new measured data.

**Function stack convention.** This page uses Ne–Fi–Te–Si. The Foundation lists Te or Ti for tertiary Thinking. Type dynamics describes a model of preferences and cannot predict action order, ability or a NERIS result.

**Editorial fiction statement.** Every scene on this page is editorial fiction used for practice in telling descriptions apart, including: a rejection letter saying the first three paragraphs wander; wanting to follow up when the editor does not reply; wanting to adjust a piece already revised many times; a co-writer saying they could not get through a section; a friend saying the piece is a bit long; sending something out with no response; repeatedly opening the dashboard to check views and comments; a paper not moving for two days; the contrast of writing in the morning and editing someone else's draft in the afternoon; and the practice of changing only three places and looking back a week later.

**Scope limits.** The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate how many people sit at either NERIS A/T end. A result should be read together with the answering environment, the tool version and recent experience, and is not for ranking ability, hiring screening or relationship prediction. Health and safety matters follow professional guidance, and clinical judgement belongs to a qualified professional. If a FermatMind report shows this suffix too, its scoring implementation is not the same as 16Personalities, and the two should not be converted directly. For the assessment method, see the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

summary_card.summary:
In ENFP-T, the -T stands for Turbulent on 16Personalities’ NERIS Identity scale. It describes a tendency toward more self-doubt and sensitivity to stress. The official MBTI uses four preference pairs and does not include this suffix. An ENFP-T result cannot tell you how creative someone is or how well they write.

ENFP stands for Extraversion, Intuition, Feeling and Perceiving. The F stands for Feeling, a preference concerning the weight of people and values in decisions. The -T after the hyphen stands for Turbulent, not Thinking.

Assertive (-A) describes greater self-assurance and less sensitivity to stress on the same scale. Two writers can make the same edit after the same feedback and feel differently about the rest of their draft.

| Item | Content |
| --- | --- |
| Type code | ENFP-T, the ENFP letters plus the Turbulent marker after the hyphen |
| Four letters | E extraversion · N intuition · F feeling · P perceiving |
| The F in third position | Feeling, a preference for giving more weight to people and values in decisions. |
| The suffix T | Turbulent, one end of the NERIS Identity |
| What T is not | Not a fifth official MBTI dimension, not Thinking, and it measures neither talent nor the quality of a piece of writing |
| NERIS term | Turbulent (-T) |
| Scope of this page | The suffix only, and self-assessment and pressure response in writing scenes |

In a fictional editorial review, two writers receive the same comments, check the same draft against the brief and make the same revision. The first three rows illustrate how their experience might differ; the last records the shared action.

| Same situation | Someone closer to Turbulent (-T) may | Someone closer to Assertive (-A) may | What the row illustrates |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Both receive the same comment about the opening | Feel less confident about the original choice of topic. | Still feel confident about the topic, even though the opening needs work. | Identity: self-assurance |
| Both confirm which paragraph the editor meant | Feel the feedback reflects on their writing more broadly. | Feel the feedback concerns that part of the draft. | Identity: scope of self-assessment |
| Both read the feedback again after making the same edit | Still feel unsettled by it. | Feel less troubled by the same feedback. | Identity: sensitivity to stress |
| Both revise the same opening | Can check each comment against the brief. | Can check each comment against the brief. | Shared action. The edit cannot establish a suffix. |

The table shows possible reactions, not criteria. The two ends often take the same action on a concrete task.

profile.excerpt: The T in ENFP-T sits to the right of the hyphen and belongs to NERIS from 16Personalities; Identity describes self-assessment and sensitivity to pressure: the T end usually doubts itself sooner and is more sensitive, while the A end usually trusts its own judgement more. In the scene of a long piece sent back, the question is how much confidence you had in that judgement while deciding what to change.

sections.title: Quick answer

sections.body_md:
Extraversion and Introversion describe whether attention and energy tend to turn outward or inward. Intuition gives more weight to patterns and possibilities, while Sensing gives more weight to concrete details and experience. Feeling and Thinking describe how someone weighs people and values or impersonal criteria in decisions. Judging favors more structure in the outside world, while Perceiving favors more room to adjust.

The T on the right belongs to another layer. Identity describes general self-assessment, self-assurance and reaction to pressure; how you see your judgement after submitting a piece is only one observable scene within it, not its whole definition. It does not rate prose, topic choice or diligence.

The third letter of ENFP is F for Feeling. In other four-letter MBTI types, a T in that position stands for Thinking. The -T in ENFP-T comes from a different framework. It describes self-assurance and responses to stress.

Turbulent describes how someone may feel about their own decisions, especially under pressure. Two writers can receive the same feedback and make the same edits, yet differ in how much confidence they retain in the rest of the draft.

In the convention used here, ENFP is Ne–Fi–Te–Si: dominant extraverted Intuition, auxiliary introverted Feeling, tertiary Thinking written as Te, and inferior introverted Sensing. The Myers & Briggs Foundation lists Te or Ti for tertiary Thinking. The -T does not change the stack, and the stack does not prescribe the order of actions.

### How ENFP-T and ENFP-A can differ after feedback

After reviewing the same comments and making the same revision, someone closer to Turbulent may feel less sure of their original judgment. Someone closer to Assertive may still trust the parts of the draft the editor did not question. Neither response tells you whether the revision was effective.

Whether to write long or short, story or argument, depends on the material and the platform's requirements, not on the right-hand letter. The same person writing in the morning and editing someone else's draft in the afternoon has changed position, and the way they close the work does not necessarily change with it.
sections.title: ENFP-T letters and framework

sections.body_md:
In a fictional editorial review, an editor says the first three paragraphs are hard to follow. Check which paragraph they marked and whether the introduction still answers the question in the headline and brief. The same comment could point to a long setup or a mismatch with the brief. Finding out which one matters more than deciding whether to defend the draft.

The table below shows writing responses that do not separate A from T. Either end may make these choices, and the action itself is no evidence for a suffix.

| Situation | A possible choice | The cost to watch | One move to try |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Just given a topic | List the things you want to say first, then think about structure | Listing too many makes the opening wander more | After listing, circle the one most relevant to the reader's question |
| Receiving revision comments | Go through your draft point by point | The comments may mix in section preferences | Ask the editor to point at one paragraph before deciding which layer to change |
| The day before the deadline | Consider rewriting the entire draft. | A rewrite can leave too little time to check the facts. | Agree what must be fixed before submission and protect time for fact-checking. |
| The editor does not reply | Want to send another follow-up | Too many follow-ups make it hard for them to answer | Ask once, and write the question so it can be answered in one line |
| The same piece already revised several times | Want every version a little better | Returns diminish and fatigue lowers judgement | Agree with the editor in advance which items count as passing |

One counterexample is worth keeping: the same person may still feel confident about the next piece when the subject is familiar and the rejection is specific, and the same event may be read as a general rejection when the subject is unfamiliar, the comments are vague and the deadline is tight. Change the conditions and the reaction changes.
sections.title: ENFP-T core patterns, value and counterexamples

sections.body_md:
Where checking effort should go depends on whether a reader can actually see a difference after the change. Worth more revision: the opening, the conclusion, and the few sentences likely to be screenshotted and quoted. Not worth repeated work: transitions and adjectives. Separate the two and the checking has a boundary, so a whole evening does not go into adjusting the feel of one paragraph.

When an editor says you went off topic, ask them to point at one paragraph: is the example off the subject, or has the conclusion wandered onto another topic? The two corrections differ, and mixing them easily overturns the whole piece.

### ENFP-T at work or study: giving revision a finishing point

Revision exists to stop real problems, so it needs a finishing point rather than a better mood.

Before submitting, go through three columns: does the argument land on the reader's question, do the examples fit the argument (can factual cases be verified, are fictional ones marked), and is there a sentence that could be misread. Once the three are done, submit, and put the remaining ideas into a note for the next piece.

If a paper has not moved for two days, decide first whether the material is insufficient or something else interrupted; fix only one of the two, then watch for a day, and do not restructure three times in one day.

If you value detailed feedback and time to revise, compare the tasks and review cycles of roles such as content editor or research assistant. A small project or internship can show whether you want to repeat that work. The suffix cannot establish career fit.
sections.title: ENFP-T work and career exploration

sections.body_md:
Co-writing a piece, the other person says "I could not get through this section", and you may hear it first as a verdict on your prose. Restate before confirming: "did you get stuck at the third paragraph, or is the order of the whole piece wrong?" Restating pulls the scope back to a specific place.

In a fictional exchange, a friend says the draft feels long. Ask where they lost the thread. If they cannot identify a passage, you can leave the cause open or ask another reader.

If a draft receives no response, ask a specific reader one question about it. A reply gives you a point to consider. Silence does not establish what they thought of the draft.

Frequency and boundaries can be stated in advance: how often you want concentrated feedback, which changes both sides must confirm, and telling the other person early when a promised time will not be met rather than letting it run to the deadline. Agreeing costs less than guessing.

### ENFP-T: landing self-assessment back on the draft

What has to land is a location, not the strength of a feeling.

Find that specific sentence: ask the collaborator to repeat the paragraph they could not get through, and see whether they stuck on the order of information or on a premise you never stated. Once the sentence is located, the change has somewhere to go; if it cannot be located, it may only have been their state that day. Do not ask the other person to keep reassuring you that it is well written — that solves nothing and drains the relationship.
sections.title: ENFP-T relationships and communication

sections.body_md:
In a fictional publishing example, two writers look at the same numbers after releasing a piece. One may remain confident about the topic, while the other feels more doubtful about their earlier judgment. Traffic and comments can inform a review, but they cannot establish someone’s ability or which suffix fits.

The data exists to judge topics, but after a short night the same number looks more and more like a verdict. Give yourself a time limit: look for ten minutes, note what needs changing, and leave the rest for tomorrow.

Another reaction is rehearsing the readers' response for them: will they think I am preaching. The rehearsed version is usually heavier than real comments. Asking one person who will actually read it is more informative than running it repeatedly in your head.

If you have slept badly for several days, opened and closed the document again and again, and traced one rejection back to yourself repeatedly, pause the repeated rework first; if it can be negotiated, adjust the submission schedule, and talk to someone you trust. If this state persists or clearly affects daily life, consider professional support. Do not use A/T to explain insomnia.
sections.title: ENFP-T stress and recovery

sections.body_md:
Use a returned draft to reflect on three things: what the editor said, what you changed and how you felt about the original judgment afterwards. This exercise cannot establish an A/T result.

Pick a rejection you remember, and compare three things: the paragraph they named, the sentence you were most reluctant to cut, and the readers' response after the change. A change in response only shows this piece changed; whether this particular edit caused it still depends on whether other paragraphs and other readers show the same shift.

Keep counterexamples too. Some people rewrite the whole piece after one rejection yet get through in one pass on a familiar subject; others are generous with other people's drafts and severe with their own. Comparing familiarity with the subject, clarity of the feedback and the cost of rework can produce an explanation to test, not a way to type anyone.

Practise one low-risk thing: next piece, change only the opening, the conclusion and the quoted sentence, then submit. A week later, check whether the places readers got stuck were those three. If two weeks of records still show no difference, or the recording itself makes you more anxious, stop.
sections.title: ENFP-T observation practice

sections.title: ENFP-T related types and comparisons

items.answer:
T is the first letter of Turbulent, from the NERIS Identity used by 16Personalities. It describes general self-assessment, self-assurance and sensitivity to pressure; it measures no talent, output or popularity with readers, and it is not a fifth official MBTI dimension.

After receiving feedback, record what the editor actually said, what you changed and how sure you felt about the original draft. The exercise can clarify how you respond to feedback. Your revision process cannot establish a suffix.
items.question: What does the T in ENFP-T mean?

items.answer:
No, they are on different layers. The third F comes from Feeling and covers judgement weighting people and values; the T on the right is Turbulent, belonging to self-assessment and pressure response.

A report that gives only four letters carries no right-hand information. Seeing -T, do not read it as Thinking either; the two Ts share a letter and belong to different frameworks.
items.question: The third letter of ENFP-T is F. Does that conflict with the T?

items.answer:
There is no such relationship. The suffix does not enter an evaluation of writing ability; whether a piece works depends on the subject, the material, the platform's standards and the editor's requirements.

The same person may rate themselves differently at the two ends while taking the same revision actions. To judge whether an edit is worth it, ask whether a reader can see a difference: the opening and conclusion deserve more work, and transitions can be let go.
items.question: Is ENFP-T necessarily a worse writer than ENFP-A?

items.answer:
Ne or Fi strength cannot be inferred from -T. Ne and Fi are theoretical preferences in type dynamics; the NERIS Identity does not measure those two processes, and the two accounts cannot be converted into each other.

Whether the writing goes well depends on how much has been read, how much practised, and whether anyone gives specific comments, all of which can be observed separately. Spotting a function requires long-term habits of sourcing and judging; the pace of one submission is no evidence.
items.question: Are Ne and Fi weakened in ENFP-T?

items.answer:
Establish which layer is being sent back before touching anything.

Restate the comment, then ask one question: is the idea off, or is the opening too convoluted. The two call for different revisions, and going the wrong way wastes a whole evening. If the answer is only "it is not quite working", ask them to mark one paragraph.
items.question: ENFP-T: when a piece is sent back, should I revise or ask first?

items.answer:
Repeated revision can help when it tests a real concern. Decide which checks the brief requires and which changes would improve the piece. A revision count tells you little about the quality of the work or the suffix.

Three columns can be listed: the argument, the examples, and the sentences that could be misread. Finish the three and submit, leaving the rest for the next piece. The next day, review by argument, evidence and risk of misreading rather than by the urge to change more.
items.question: ENFP-T: does repeated revision count as being conscientious?

items.answer:
Yes. Getting through in one pass depends on whether the piece met the requirements; even after a rejection, a familiar subject, clear comments or enough time may leave someone little affected. Neither one-pass acceptance nor the reaction to one rejection can determine A/T.

To observe this, record the conditions at the time: how familiar the subject was, how clear the comments were, and how much time was left. With different conditions, the reaction differs anyway.
items.question: Can Someone With an ENFP-T Result Feel Confident After One Review?

items.answer:
It depends on whether you need the base or the other end.

The four letters in full are on the [ENFP profile](/en/personality/enfp); the A end is [ENFP-A](/en/personality/enfp-a); both ends side by side are on the [same-type comparison](/en/personality/enfp-a-vs-enfp-t).
items.question: What Should I Read Next About ENFP-T?

sections.body_md:
**Framework sources.** The suffix follows [the 16Personalities account of NERIS](https://www.16personalities.com/articles/our-theory); the four letters and the four-position description follow the public material of the MBTI framework, and this page introduces no new measured data.

**Function stack convention.** This page uses Ne–Fi–Te–Si. The Foundation lists Te or Ti for tertiary Thinking. Type dynamics describes a model of preferences and cannot predict action order, ability or a NERIS result.

**Editorial fiction statement.** Every scene on this page is editorial fiction used for practice in telling descriptions apart, including: a rejection letter saying the first three paragraphs wander; wanting to follow up when the editor does not reply; wanting to adjust a piece already revised many times; a co-writer saying they could not get through a section; a friend saying the piece is a bit long; sending something out with no response; repeatedly opening the dashboard to check views and comments; a paper not moving for two days; the contrast of writing in the morning and editing someone else's draft in the afternoon; and the practice of changing only three places and looking back a week later.

**Scope limits.** The four-letter sample distribution of MBTI Form M cannot be used to estimate how many people sit at either NERIS A/T end. A result should be read together with the answering environment, the tool version and recent experience, and is not for ranking ability, hiring screening or relationship prediction. Health and safety matters follow professional guidance, and clinical judgement belongs to a qualified professional. If a FermatMind report shows this suffix too, its scoring implementation is not the same as 16Personalities, and the two should not be converted directly. For the assessment method, see the [scoring and evidence notes](/en/tests/mbti-personality-test-16-personality-types#method-and-evidence).

FermatMind Editorial
